newsitem.title: UK: UK inflation raises prospect of pre-poll rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK inflation raises prospect of pre-poll rate rise.

text.p: A leap in underlying UK inflation in October has raised the chances of a further interest rate rise before elections due by May 1997, analysts said.
The jump in RPIX inflation to 3.3 percent year-on-year, coupled with a spectacular fall in unemployment last month, means December's monetary meeting will be highly charged.
"I don't think Clarke would do it in December and there is a chance he will hold out until May, but it must raise the chances of a pre-election rate rise," said UBS economist Alex Garrard.

But the very fact that analysts are talking about the possibility of an interest rate rise after Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's December 11 meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George, shows how much the monetary policy debate has moved.
When Clarke raised base rates by a quarter-point to 6.00 percent last month, most economists were caught unawares. But now it seems it might have been the first in a succession of increases.
"Coupled with the labour data, the RPI will raise market fears that Clarke's behind the curve," Garrard said.
British jobless queues were cut by more than 40,000 last month, taking the unemployment rate to a five-and-a-half-year low of 7.2 percent.

Alongside underlying inflation's jump, the headline rate leapt to 2.7 percent year-on-year from 2.1. Garrard said the government's medium-term target of 2.5 percent for underlying inflation was now an unattainable dream.

Chancellor Clarke released a statement on the figures saying the annual rise in inflation was due to an exceptional fall in RPI last year falling out of the equation. Headline retail prices fell by 0.5 percent in October 1995.

Clarke added that government policy was still set to meet the inflation target. Andrew Snowball, economist at the Cooperative Bank, said if that was Clarke's objective the chances of a December 11 rate rise were significantly increased.
"The numbers are bad whichever way you look at them," he said. "They reflect not only price falls from a year ago dropping out of the equation but also fresh price increases in many areas."
Thursday's figures showed motoring prices, including petrol, rose by 0.6 percent in October while housing costs grew 1.5 percent year-on-year, up from 0.1 in September.
Those exerted the main upward pressure on the overall index, the Office for National Statistics said.
One of the worrying factors for UK markets was the failure of clothing and footwear prices to fall in October, despite their 5.2 percent leap in September.
"The expected monthly fallback in clothing and footwear prices failed to materialise," Garrard said. That suggested those retailers were trying to push through higher prices.
"They are trying it on," Garrard said.
There is little doubt how the Bank of England will view this week's economic statistics.
In last week's quarterly inflation report, the Bank said the government's 2.5 percent inflation target was unlikely to be met and rates would probably have to rise again.
Bank governor Eddie George hammered that message home at the Confederation of British Industry's annual conference, earlier this week.

"The BoE will certainly claim this report to be consistent with their calls for higher borrowing costs now," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica. "Speculation will certainly be on a 6.25 percent base rate at the next monetary meeting in December."
